Lesson 12 showed agencies making binding rules through notice and comment, and Lesson 13 showed the FDA doing it. Today's question is simpler: can a president or a government just order things, without passing a law or running a rulemaking? Each country answers "yes, but only inside a box", and the shape of the box is what matters.

**The US: orders from Article II.** An **executive order** is a written, signed directive from the president to the executive branch. The Constitution never mentions executive orders. Presidents draw them from Article II, which vests "the executive power" in the president and tells him to see that the laws are faithfully executed, and from powers Congress has delegated by statute. Orders are numbered and published in the Federal Register. They can direct agencies, reorganise how work is done, set conditions for federal contracts and start rulemakings, but they cannot create new crimes, spend money Congress has not appropriated or override a statute.

> Numbering began in 1907, when the State Department retroactively labelled an 1862 order by [@Abraham Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln) as Executive Order 1.

**Three limits.** First, **the courts**. In the [#Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youngstown_Sheet_%26_Tube_Co._v._Sawyer) case of 1952, Justice [@Robert H. Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_H._Jackson) set out the test still used today: a president is strongest when acting with Congress's authorisation, in a "zone of twilight" when Congress is silent, and weakest when acting against Congress's will. Second, **Congress**, which can pass a law reversing an order, though the president can veto it (Lesson 7) and an override needs two-thirds. Congress can also refuse to fund what an order requires. Third, **the next president**, who can revoke an order with a stroke of the pen. That makes orders fast but fragile; policy built on them often flips when the White House changes hands.

**Poland: no free-floating decrees.** Poland's president has no general power to govern by order. Most of his official acts need the **countersignature** (kontrasygnata) of the prime minister, who thereby takes political responsibility for them before the Sejm. Only a closed list of **prerogatives** escapes that rule, such as appointing the prime minister, nominating judges, calling elections or referring laws to the Constitutional Tribunal. The government's tools are tighter still. A ministerial **regulation** (rozporządzenie) is binding on everyone but may be issued only on a specific authorisation in an act of parliament, a topic for Lesson 15. Resolutions of the Council of Ministers and **orders of the prime minister** (zarządzenia) are internal: they bind only the offices beneath them and cannot be the legal basis for decisions about citizens.

> The 1997 Constitution, adopted by referendum, lists the President's 30 prerogatives in Article 144(3).

**India: executive power follows legislative power.** Under Article 73, the Union government's executive power reaches every subject on which Parliament can legislate. The Supreme Court has read this to mean the government may act by **executive order** where no law yet exists, so long as it does not breach fundamental rights or contradict a statute. All such action is taken formally in the President's name (Article 77), but under Article 74 the President acts on ministers' advice, so the real author is the cabinet. Orders usually appear as **office memoranda**, resolutions or notifications in the Gazette of India. India also has a much stronger tool, the **ordinance**, a temporary law the President can issue when Parliament is not sitting; that gets its own lesson (17).

> The Allocation of Business Rules, which divide work among ministries, were issued by the President in 1961 under Article 77(3).

**The pattern.** The US gives its president the widest room to act alone, then relies on courts, Congress and elections to push back. Poland ties most presidential acts to a government answerable to the Sejm and lets ministers bind citizens only when a law says so. India sits between: broad executive power on paper, exercised by a cabinet that must keep a majority in the Lok Sabha. Scholars still argue over how far each system's executive can stretch, and the US debate in particular has grown sharper as recent presidents have leaned on orders when Congress is divided.

items.example: In April 1952, with the [#Korean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War) under way and a national steel strike looming, President [@Harry S. Truman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman) issued an executive order directing his Commerce Secretary to seize and run the country's steel mills. He cited his powers as commander in chief, not any statute; Congress had in fact rejected seizure powers when it passed the Taft–Hartley Act. The companies sued, and within two months the Supreme Court ruled 6–3 against him in [#Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youngstown_Sheet_%26_Tube_Co._v._Sawyer). The majority held that the president cannot make law; Justice [@Robert H. Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_H._Jackson)'s concurrence added the three-zone test. The mills went back to their owners and the strike resumed. The case remains the starting point whenever a president acts alone against Congress's wishes.

In Poland, President [@Karol Nawrocki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karol_Nawrocki) appointed [@Andrzej Domański](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrzej_Doma%C5%84ski) deputy prime minister, an act taken on the prime minister's motion rather than on the President's own initiative.

items.body:
Last week asked how a majority turns into law. This week asked two different questions: how majorities are won, and how power is shared out once they are, between the centre and the regions, and between lawmakers and the officials who run things day to day.

**Winning the seats.** Lesson 9 showed that the counting rule shapes the whole system. First-past-the-post gives the US two big parties and gives India a crowd of regional parties that dominate their own states, which is why Uttar Pradesh's 2027 assembly race already fills the Indian news. Poland's proportional Sejm almost guarantees coalitions, and the Electoral College explains why American campaigns live in a handful of swing states. The November midterms that hand Democrats both houses of Congress in January set up much of what followed.

**Sharing power downward.** Lessons 10 and 11 split the world into federal and unitary states. US states hold powers the [#Tenth Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution) reserves to them; India divides powers into Union, State and Concurrent lists; Poland lends its regions and towns real powers by ordinary statute. Kraków showed what that looks like up close: the mayor drafts an 11.9bn zł budget and fare plans, but nothing becomes local law without the 43-member City Council. This weekend's arrests by federal immigration agents at Seattle's airport, condemned by Washington state and port officials, show the federal line from the other side: states can protest, but immigration is a federal power they cannot override.

> Poland's elected local governments were reborn in the [#1990 Polish local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_Polish_local_elections), held in May 1990.

**Sharing power sideways.** Lessons 12 to 14 followed rules that are not written by legislatures. US agencies make binding rules through notice and comment under the [#Administrative Procedure Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrative_Procedure_Act), as with CMS's anti-fraud proposal now open for comment, or take the faster interim-final route that Commerce used for AI-chip exports, which matters for Poland's access to advanced chips. The FDA showed the gap between a binding regulation and guidance that companies follow anyway. Then executive orders: [@Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump)'s 20 November order on contractors and congressional requests will be judged by the zones of [#Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youngstown_Sheet_%26_Tube_Co._v._Sawyer). In Poland, by contrast, President [@Karol Nawrocki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karol_Nawrocki) has no general power to govern by order, and most of his acts need the prime minister's countersignature.

**The thread.** In every country, the people who actually make a rule are often not the ones voters chose for that job: a city council rather than parliament, an agency rather than Congress, a president's pen rather than a statute. Each lesson asked the same follow-up: who gave them that power, and who can take it back? Next week moves on to Polish acts and regulations, then to the EU, where that question gets a fourth layer.

items.body:
Lesson 12 showed US agencies turning statutes into binding rules, and Lesson 14 ended with a Polish rule: a minister can bind citizens only if an act of parliament says so. Today we open that box. Poland's legal system is built as a strict ladder, and each rung may only do what the rung above allows.

**The closed list.** Article 87 of the 1997 Constitution names the sources of universally binding law: the Constitution, **statutes** (ustawy), ratified international agreements and **regulations** (rozporządzenia). Add **acts of local law** (akty prawa miejscowego), which bind only inside the territory of the council or voivode that made them. Anything else, such as a prime minister's order or a cabinet resolution, binds only offices inside the government. This list is deliberately closed: a citizen can check whether a rule really binds them by asking which rung it sits on.

**Acts versus regulations.** An **act** (ustawa) is passed by the Sejm and Senate and signed by the President, the path you met in Lesson 6. Only an act may restrict a constitutional freedom (Article 31(3)), impose a tax or define a crime. A **regulation** is issued by a minister, the Council of Ministers or the prime minister, and it fills in the details: forms, deadlines, technical standards, fee amounts. Under Article 92 it needs a **specific authorisation** (upoważnienie ustawowe) in an act, which must name who issues the regulation, what it may cover and guidelines for its content. The minister cannot hand that power to someone else, and the regulation cannot go beyond the authorisation. If it does, the Constitutional Tribunal (Lesson 8) can strike it down, and ordinary courts may simply refuse to apply it in a case.

**No rule without publication.** Article 88 says acts, regulations and local law take effect only once promulgated. National acts and regulations appear in **Dziennik Ustaw** (the Journal of Laws). The standard waiting period, the **vacatio legis**, is 14 days after publication unless the act sets another date, so that people can learn the rule before it bites. Acts that bind only the administration go in a separate journal, **Monitor Polski**, while each voivodeship has its own official journal for local law, such as Kraków city council resolutions.

> Dziennik Ustaw traces its line to a journal of laws first published in Warsaw in 1918. Publishing it is the Prime Minister's responsibility, and since 2012 the electronic edition has been the official one.

**How this compares.** The US and India use the same idea, delegated or subordinate legislation, but police it differently. In the US, Congress must give agencies an "intelligible principle", and since [#Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loper_Bright_Enterprises_v._Raimondo) in 2024 courts no longer defer to an agency's reading of an unclear statute. In India, ministries issue **rules** under a parent act, publish them in the Gazette of India and lay them before Parliament, where a Committee on Subordinate Legislation in each House checks that they stay within the act. Poland writes the limits into the Constitution itself, which makes the question "is there a specific authorisation?" the first one any Polish lawyer asks.

**Why it matters.** Polish governments often reach for regulations because they are quick: no Sejm votes, no presidential veto. That speed is exactly why the courts watch them. When a regulation does something only an act may do, it is the regulation that falls, however urgent the reason. Scholars and politicians still disagree over how detailed an authorisation must be, and the Tribunal's answer has shifted from case to case.

items.example: In spring 2020, during the [#COVID-19 pandemic in Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Poland), the government restricted movement, gatherings and business through Council of Ministers regulations issued under the act on infectious diseases. It chose not to declare a constitutional state of natural disaster, which would have allowed rights to be limited more widely. Thousands of people were fined. The then Ombudsman, [@Adam Bodnar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Bodnar), appealed many of these cases. In March 2021 the Supreme Court set aside the first three fines, and lawyers widely read the rulings as confirming that a regulation cannot restrict a constitutional freedom on its own: Article 31(3) reserves that for an act. Administrative courts reached similar results on fines imposed by sanitary inspectors. The government argued it had acted lawfully in an emergency; the episode became a textbook case of a regulation reaching beyond its statute.

Lessons 12 to 15 were about who writes the rules. Today's lesson is about a body that writes almost none of them, yet moves markets more than any ministry: the **central bank**. All three countries have one, and all three have tried to answer the same question: how do you give unelected experts power over the price of money and still keep them accountable?

**What a central bank does.** It issues the currency, keeps the banking system liquid (it is the **lender of last resort** when banks panic), usually supervises banks, and above all sets the **policy interest rate**: the rate at which it lends to or borrows from commercial banks. Raise that rate and loans, mortgages and credit cards get dearer, spending cools and inflation should fall, at the cost of slower growth. Cut it and the reverse happens. A higher rate also tends to make a currency more attractive to foreign savers, which is why rate decisions and exchange rates appear in the same headlines.

**The Federal Reserve.** The Fed is a creature of statute, not of the Constitution. A seven-member **Board of Governors** in Washington is appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate for 14-year terms; the chair serves a renewable four-year term, held since May 2026 by [@Kevin Warsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Warsh). Rates are set by the **Federal Open Market Committee** (FOMC): the seven governors, the president of the New York Fed, who always votes, and four of the other eleven regional bank presidents in rotation. Congress gave the Fed a **dual mandate**, maximum employment and stable prices, and the Fed itself chose to define stable prices as 2% inflation.

> The Fed was created by the [#Federal Reserve Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Act), signed by [@Woodrow Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson) in December 1913, a response to the [#Panic of 1907](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1907).

**Narodowy Bank Polski.** Poland is the only one of the three to write its central bank into the Constitution. Article 227 gives NBP the exclusive right to issue money and to make and carry out monetary policy, and makes it responsible for the value of the złoty. The NBP president (currently [@Adam Glapiński](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Glapi%C5%84ski)) is elected by the Sejm on the President's motion for six years. Rates are set by the **Monetary Policy Council** (Rada Polityki Pieniężnej, RPP): the NBP president plus nine members, three each chosen by the President, the Sejm and the Senate, for single six-year terms. The split appointment is a deliberate check: no single branch can pack the council. The RPP set its own target of 2.5% inflation, give or take one point.

> NBP was founded in 1945; its interwar predecessor, Bank Polski, opened in 1924 during [@Władysław Grabski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W%C5%82adys%C5%82aw_Grabski)'s reform that introduced the złoty.

**The Reserve Bank of India.** The RBI also rests on an ordinary law, and for most of its history the governor decided rates alone. A 2016 amendment created a six-member **Monetary Policy Committee** (MPC): three from the RBI, including the governor, who has a casting vote, and three outside experts appointed by the central government. Unlike in the US or Poland, the **government sets the target** — 4% consumer inflation, with a band of 2 to 6% — and the RBI must explain itself in writing if it misses the band for three quarters in a row.

> The RBI opened on 1 April 1935 in Calcutta under the [#Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reserve_Bank_of_India_Act,_1934); it began as a shareholder-owned bank and was nationalised in 1949.

**Independence is a spectrum.** Economists generally argue that a central bank shielded from politicians fights inflation more credibly, because voters reward cheap money before elections. Critics reply that such independence leaves big distributive choices with officials nobody elected. Each country sits at a different point: Poland protects its bank in the Constitution; the US relies on long terms and a statute Congress could change; India's government chooses the target, appoints half the committee and, under section 7 of the RBI Act, may issue directions to the bank after consulting the governor. That last point matters for Lesson 16: if Poland ever adopted the euro, rate-setting would pass from the RPP to the European Central Bank in Frankfurt.

items.title: The EU: what Brussels decides vs Warsaw; regulations vs directives
items.body:
Lesson 15 showed how Warsaw makes rules: the Sejm passes acts, ministers issue regulations under them, and everything is published in Dziennik Ustaw. But a large share of the rules that actually govern Polish shops, farms and phones were not written in Warsaw at all. They were agreed in Brussels, and Poland had a seat at the table. Today's lesson is about that second layer, and why it has no real equivalent in the US or India.

**Pooled sovereignty.** The European Union is not a federation like the US, and not just a treaty club either. Member states have handed some powers to shared institutions while keeping the rest. The treaties sort powers into three groups. **Exclusive competences**, such as trade policy, customs and competition rules for the single market, belong to the EU alone: Poland cannot sign its own trade deal with India or the US. **Shared competences**, such as the internal market, environment, energy and consumer protection, can be regulated by both, but once the EU acts, national law must follow. Everything else stays national: taxes on income, the army, schools, healthcare organisation and most criminal law.

> Poland joined on 1 May 2004 in the [#2004 enlargement of the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_enlargement_of_the_European_Union), after 77% voted yes in the [#2003 Polish European Union membership referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_Polish_European_Union_membership_referendum).

**Who decides.** The **European Commission** proposes laws and enforces them; Poland names one of its 27 commissioners. The **Council of the EU**, made up of national ministers, and the directly elected **European Parliament** amend and pass them, usually together. The **European Council** of presidents and prime ministers sets direction and settles the hardest deals, such as the seven-year budget. The **Court of Justice** in Luxembourg has the final word on what EU law means. So when a Polish minister votes in the Council, Warsaw is not being overruled by outsiders: it is one vote among 27, weighted by population, and sometimes it loses.

**Regulations vs directives.** This is the distinction to remember. A **regulation** applies directly in every member state the day it takes effect, with no Polish act needed, much like a US federal statute binds every state. A **directive** sets a goal and a deadline, and each country must **transpose** it into its own law, so in Poland a directive becomes a Sejm act or ministerial regulation in Dziennik Ustaw. In practice the line blurs: even a regulation often needs a national act to name the authority that enforces it and set penalties. That is exactly what the vetoed Polish act implementing the Digital Services Act was for.

**Which law wins?** Since [#Flaminio Costa v E.N.E.L.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flaminio_Costa_v_E.N.E.L.) in 1964, the Court of Justice has held that EU law takes precedence over conflicting national law. Poland's Constitution accepts this partly: Article 90 allows powers to be transferred by treaty, and Article 91 gives such law priority over ordinary statutes, but the Constitution itself is treated as supreme. In case K 3/21 in October 2021, the Constitutional Tribunal ruled some treaty provisions unconstitutional as the Court of Justice interpreted them. Supporters saw a defence of sovereignty; the Commission and many lawyers saw a breach of EU law, and the dispute is still not fully settled.

**The comparison.** Neither the US nor India belongs to anything like this. Their closest parallel is internal: the split between Washington and the states, or between New Delhi and the states under the three lists, from Lesson 10. India's Union List gives trade and foreign affairs to the centre, just as the treaties give trade to Brussels. The difference is that the EU's "centre" is a body its members created and can, in theory, leave, as [#Brexit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit) showed.

> The EU's legal roots go back to the [#Treaty of Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Rome) of 1957; its current shape comes from the [#Maastricht Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maastricht_Treaty) (1992) and the [#Treaty of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Lisbon) (2009).

items.example: The EU's 2021–2027 budget showed the system at its most dramatic. Spending of about €1.8 trillion, including the COVID recovery fund, needed **unanimity** among national leaders. A new **rule-of-law conditionality** regulation let the Commission cut funds to a state that misused EU money through weak courts or corruption. In November 2020 Poland and Hungary vetoed the whole package in protest. The December 2020 [#European Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Council) found a compromise: the regulation stayed, but would not be used until the Court of Justice ruled on it. The Court upheld it in 2022. Poland's recovery funds were then frozen over judicial reforms until 2024, when the new government of [@Donald Tusk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Tusk) committed to changes and the money was released. Historians and politicians in Poland still disagree on whether this was legitimate pressure or overreach.
items.inTheNews: Tusk's red lines before Thursday's extraordinary European Council show the unanimity rule at work: the 2028–2034 budget cannot pass without Poland, so Warsaw has real leverage. Reported US Section 301 tariffs name "the EU" as one target because trade is decided in Brussels, not Warsaw, while India negotiates for itself; meanwhile the vetoed Polish act implementing the [#Digital Services Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Services_Act) shows that even a directly applicable regulation needs national enforcement rules.

check.q: Poland wants to cut tariffs on Indian textiles on its own. Why can't it?
options: The Sejm would need a two-thirds majority
Trade policy is an exclusive EU competence, so only the EU can set tariffs
India does not trade with individual EU states
The President of Poland must approve all tariffs
check.explain: Customs and trade policy belong to the EU alone. The Commission negotiates and the EU sets common external tariffs for all 27 members.

check.q: An EU directive on packaging waste is adopted. What happens in Poland?
options: It applies automatically the next day with no Polish law
It applies only if the Constitutional Tribunal approves it
Poland must transpose it into its own law by the deadline, choosing the method
It is advisory and Poland may ignore it
check.explain: A directive binds the state as to the result but leaves the form to national authorities, so the Sejm or a minister must write it into Polish law. Missing the deadline can lead to Commission infringement action.

check.q: Why can one member state hold up the EU's seven-year budget?
options: Because the European Parliament votes by country
Because the MFF needs unanimity among governments in the Council
Because the Commission needs every commissioner's signature
Because each state's constitutional court must approve it
check.explain: The treaties require the Council to adopt the MFF unanimously, after the European Parliament consents. That gives each government a veto, as Poland and Hungary used in 2020.

items.recallQ: What is the practical difference between an EU regulation and an EU directive, and why did Poland still need a national act to implement the Digital Services Act, which is a regulation?
items.recallA: A regulation applies directly in every member state as soon as it takes effect, while a directive sets a goal that each state must transpose into its own law by a deadline. Even a regulation often leaves states to designate the enforcing authority and set procedures and penalties, so Poland needed an act to make the Digital Services Act enforceable in practice; that is the act President Nawrocki vetoed.

items.body:
Lessons 15 and 16 traced how Warsaw and Brussels turn laws into detailed rules. India's machinery looks familiar at first: Parliament passes acts, ministries write rules under them, and everything is published in an official gazette. But India's Constitution adds one tool that neither the US nor peacetime Poland has: the power of the executive to make law on its own, for a limited time, while the legislature is away.

**Ordinances.** Under **Article 123**, when either House of Parliament is not sitting, the President can promulgate an **ordinance** if satisfied that circumstances require immediate action. As Lesson 3 showed, "the President" in practice means the Union Cabinet, which advises and binds the President. An ordinance has the same force as an act of Parliament and can cover anything Parliament could legislate on. **Article 213** gives each state's Governor the same power for state subjects. The safeguard is a clock: once Parliament reassembles, the ordinance must be laid before both Houses, and it lapses six weeks later unless Parliament passes a replacement bill. Since Parliament must meet at least every six months, an ordinance can live roughly seven and a half months at most.

> The ordinance power was carried over from the [#Government of India Act 1935](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_India_Act_1935); [@B. R. Ambedkar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._R._Ambedkar) defended keeping it in the Constituent Assembly as a tool for emergencies.

**Abuse and the courts.** Governments have often used ordinances to skip debate, especially when they lacked a majority in the Rajya Sabha. Bihar became the classic case: between 1967 and 1981 it issued 256 ordinances and kept some alive for years by simply reissuing them. In D.C. Wadhwa v State of Bihar (1986) the Supreme Court called this a subversion of democracy, and in Krishna Kumar Singh v State of Bihar (2017) a seven-judge bench went further: repeated re-promulgation, especially without placing ordinances before the legislature, is a fraud on the Constitution, and the President's or Governor's "satisfaction" can be reviewed by courts in limited cases. Defenders still argue the tool is needed when urgent action cannot wait for a session.

**Subordinate legislation and the Gazette.** Most Indian rules, as in Poland and the US, come from delegated power. An act lets the government make **rules**, **regulations** or **notifications**, and they take effect when printed in the **Gazette of India** (today published online as the e-Gazette), or a state gazette for state rules. Rules must be laid before Parliament, where each House's Committee on Subordinate Legislation checks they stay within the parent act. Unlike the US, India has no binding notice-and-comment law: a 2014 Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy asks ministries to publish drafts for 30 days, but courts do not enforce it, so consultation varies.

**Regulators.** India also hands rulemaking to statutory regulators created by acts of Parliament: the RBI for banking (Lesson 18), SEBI for securities, TRAI for telecoms, the Competition Commission of India and FSSAI for food safety. Each issues binding regulations within its field, much like the SEC or FCC in the US, or Poland's financial supervisor KNF.

> SEBI was set up in 1988 and given statutory powers in 1992, after the [#1992 Indian stock market scam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_Indian_stock_market_scam) linked to [@Harshad Mehta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harshad_Mehta).

**The comparison.** In the US, a president who wants to act fast can issue executive orders, but (as Lesson 14 showed) they cannot create new law, and courts strike them down when they try. Poland's Constitution allows the President to issue regulations with the force of statute only under martial law when the Sejm cannot meet (Article 234). India's ordinance is the only peacetime executive lawmaking power of the three, which is why its limits matter so much.

items.example: In June 2020, during the pandemic and with Parliament not sitting, the government of [@Narendra Modi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narendra_Modi) issued three ordinances changing how farm produce is sold. When Parliament returned in September, it passed them as the [#2020 Indian agriculture acts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Indian_agriculture_acts), with the Rajya Sabha approving two of them by a disputed voice vote. Critics said using ordinances first had denied states and farmers any consultation on what is largely a state subject; the government said reform was urgent. The [#2020–2021 Indian farmers' protest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020–2021_Indian_farmers'_protest) camped on Delhi's borders for a year, the Supreme Court suspended the laws in January 2021, and in November 2021 Parliament repealed them. The episode shows both the speed an ordinance gives and the political cost of skipping debate.
items.inTheNews: Today's Union Cabinet approval of an ₹11,000 crore equipment-manufacturing scheme is executive action under existing powers that needs no new law. MeitY's AI regulation consultation papers, said to be nearly final, show India's non-binding consultation habit at work, and India marks Constitution Day, the anniversary of the text that created the ordinance power.

check.q: Parliament is in recess and the Cabinet wants an urgent change to an act. What can it do, and what limits apply?
options: Nothing: only Parliament can change an act
Advise the President to issue an ordinance, which lapses six weeks after Parliament reassembles unless replaced by an act
Ask the Supreme Court to amend the act
Issue an executive order that permanently amends the act
check.explain: Article 123 lets the President, on the Cabinet's advice, make an ordinance with the force of law during a recess. It must be laid before Parliament and dies six weeks after reassembly unless Parliament passes a bill.

check.q: Why did the Supreme Court object to Bihar's practice in D.C. Wadhwa?
options: Bihar issued ordinances on Union List subjects
Bihar's Governor issued ordinances without the Cabinet's advice
Bihar kept ordinances alive for years by reissuing them instead of letting the legislature decide
Bihar failed to publish ordinances in the Gazette
check.explain: An ordinance is meant as a stopgap. Reissuing it again and again replaces the legislature with the executive, which the Court called a subversion of the democratic process.

check.q: How does consultation on draft rules in India differ from the US?
options: India requires longer comment periods
In India, consultation under the 2014 policy is not legally enforceable, while US agencies face binding notice-and-comment rules
India bans public comment on draft rules
The US has no consultation on federal rules
check.explain: The US Administrative Procedure Act makes notice-and-comment a legal requirement that courts enforce. India's Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy is guidance, so ministries vary in how much they consult.

items.body:
Every lesson so far has been about who makes rules. This one is about who controls the money, which is where much of the real power sits. All three countries agree on the basic principle, inherited from British parliamentary history: the government may spend only what the legislature approves. Where they differ is in who writes the budget, who can change it, and what happens when it is late.

**The US: Congress holds the purse.** The president sends a budget request each spring, but it is only a proposal. Spending is set by Congress through annual **appropriations** bills, traditionally twelve of them, which must pass both the House and the Senate and be signed (or survive a veto, as Lesson 7 showed). The fiscal year starts on 1 October. When the bills are not ready, Congress passes a **continuing resolution** (CR), a stopgap that keeps money flowing at roughly last year's levels. If neither happens, the **[#Antideficiency Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antideficiency_Act)** forbids agencies to spend money that has not been appropriated, so non-essential work stops: a **shutdown**. Because the Senate filibuster usually means 60 votes are needed, the minority party has leverage, and deadlines turn into standoffs.

> The 1 October fiscal year dates from the [#Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Budget_and_Impoundment_Control_Act_of_1974), which also created the Congressional Budget Office.

**Poland: the government writes, the Sejm amends within limits.** Only the Council of Ministers may introduce the budget act (Article 221 of the Constitution), and it must send the draft to the Sejm by 30 September. The Sejm can move money around, but under Article 220 its amendments may not raise the deficit above what the government proposed. The Senate has 20 days to propose changes, which the Sejm can reject. The budget is the one bill the President **cannot veto**: he must sign it within seven days, though he may also refer it to the Constitutional Tribunal (Lesson 8). Crucially, Poland has no shutdown. If the budget act is not in force on 1 January, the government runs on its draft. The pressure point is different: if the Sejm fails to get a budget to the President within four months of receiving the draft, the President may dissolve the Sejm (Article 225).

**India: the Lok Sabha decides, the Rajya Sabha advises.** Article 112 calls the budget the **Annual Financial Statement**, and the Finance Minister presents it to Parliament, now on 1 February for a fiscal year starting 1 April. The Lok Sabha then votes on **demands for grants**, ministry by ministry, and passes an **Appropriation Bill**; taxes come in the **Finance Bill**. Both are money bills, so the Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes within 14 days, and the Lok Sabha may ignore them (Lesson 5). If the full budget cannot pass before April, Parliament grants a **vote on account** to cover a few months. Losing a budget vote would, by convention, mean the government has lost the House's confidence, which is why it rarely comes close.

> The budget date moved from the last day of February to 1 February in 2017 under Finance Minister [@Arun Jaitley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arun_Jaitley), who also merged the separate rail budget into it.

**The pattern.** In the two parliamentary systems, the government controls the majority and the budget is the moment that proves it: failure triggers a crisis of confidence or an early election, not a closure of public offices. In the US, separation of powers means a president and Congress can disagree with no mechanism forcing a deal, so the default when time runs out is a stoppage. That design is why Americans know the word shutdown and Poles and Indians mostly do not.

items.example: The [#2025 United States federal government shutdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_United_States_federal_government_shutdown) began on 1 October 2025, when Democrats in the Senate withheld the votes needed for a continuing resolution, demanding an extension of health insurance subsidies. It lasted 43 days, the longest in US history, ending on 12 November. Hundreds of thousands of federal employees were furloughed or worked without pay, air traffic was cut at major airports and food aid payments were disrupted. Poland shows the contrast: in January 2025 President [@Andrzej Duda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrzej_Duda), sharply at odds with the government, still had to sign its budget, and could only refer parts of it to the Constitutional Tribunal. The money kept flowing either way. Funding lapses returned in the US in 2026 (see [#2026 United States federal government shutdowns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_United_States_federal_government_shutdowns)).
items.inTheNews: EU leaders failed to agree the 2028–2034 EU budget overnight, with Poland objecting to sending ETS revenue to Brussels; at home, the Sejm is scheduled to pass Poland's 2027 budget act (deficit planned above 281 billion zł) on 4 December, while the current US stopgap funding runs out on 11 December.

check.q: Poland's President strongly opposes the government's budget. What can he do?
options: Veto it and send it back to the Sejm
Refuse to sign it, which shuts down public offices
Sign it within seven days, and optionally refer it to the Constitutional Tribunal
Dissolve the Sejm immediately
check.explain: Article 224 requires the President to sign the budget act within seven days; it is the one bill he cannot veto, though he may ask the Tribunal to review it.

check.q: Why can the US have government shutdowns while Poland and India effectively cannot?
options: The US has no written constitution on spending
US law forbids spending without appropriations and there is no fallback, while Poland runs on the draft and India uses a vote on account
Polish and Indian courts approve budgets automatically
Only the US has a bicameral legislature
check.explain: The Antideficiency Act bars unappropriated spending, and separation of powers means nothing forces a deal. Poland's Constitution lets the government operate on its draft, and India's Lok Sabha grants interim money through a vote on account.

check.q: India's Rajya Sabha wants to cut defence spending in the Appropriation Bill. What happens?
options: The cut takes effect immediately
A joint sitting resolves the dispute
It can only recommend the change within 14 days, and the Lok Sabha may ignore it
The President decides
check.explain: The Appropriation Bill is a money bill, so under Article 109 the Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations, which the Lok Sabha is free to reject.

items.recallQ: What limit does Poland's Constitution place on the Sejm when it amends the government's budget, and what happens if the budget is not in force on 1 January?
items.recallA: Under Article 220, the Sejm's amendments may not raise the deficit above the level in the government's draft. If the budget act is not in force at the start of the year, the government operates on the basis of its draft, so there is no shutdown; if the Sejm fails to deliver a budget within four months, the President may dissolve it.
